item.title: Cabinet agrees 11th-hour budget deal without opposition support
item.description:
Cabinet agrees 11th-hour budget deal without opposition support

September 1, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The coalition parties D66, CDA and VVD have agreed a draft budget package after a marathon weekend of ”tough” and “intensive” talks.

Finance minister Eelco Heinen said the negotiations had produced a “budget for 10 parties”, but the minority government was unable to secure the approval of opposition parties before the plans are presented to parliament on September 15.

Instead the three coalition partners had to resolve their own differences on issues such as welfare cuts, changes to the system for taxing wealth and assets and the higher excess charge on health insurance.

Heinen and prime minister Rob Jetten did not disclose what concessions had been made during the negotiations, but party leaders said they had produced a balanced package designed to appeal to both left and right.

Jetten acknowledged the negotiations had been “tough” at times. “Occasionally there was a bit of friction, but that gave us a more polished budget,” he said.

Dilan Yesilgöz, leader of the VVD, said in a post on X that the cabinet had produced a budget “that can take the Netherlands forward”, while emphasising her party’s campaign points.

“The VVD wil always stand for lower taxes, room for economic growth and a government that spends less.” Earlier Yesilgöz described the negotiations as “long and intensive”.

We zijn eruit. Na lange en intensieve onderhandelingen ligt er een begroting waarmee Nederland vooruit kan. De VVD staat daarbij altijd voor lagere lasten, ruimte voor economische groei en een overheid die minder uitgeeft.

In een kabinet betekent verantwoordelijkheid nemen ook:…

— Dilan Yesilgöz – Zegerius (@DilanYesilgoz) August 31, 2026

Henri Bontenbal, leader of the CDA, said: “My aim was to come up with a good offer to the opposition. I think we’ve managed that.”

Minority government

Jetten and Heinen spent two weeks talking to opposition party leaders behind closed doors to try to secure their support for the budget before the draft package was sent to the Council of State.

But those negotiations broke down at the end of last week without producing a formal deal, meaning the cabinet will have to find the votes as the bills pass through parliament in the autumn.

The government is 10 seats short of a majority in the Lower House and 16 short in the smaller Senate, where it needs the support of at least two opposition parties.

The original deadline of last Friday was extended over the weekend and into an extra cabinet meeting on Monday afternoon as the divisions within the coalition became harder to reconcile.

The centre parties, D66 and CDA, wanted to scrap some of the proposed €6.5 billion budget cuts planned for the next four years to appeal to Progressief Nederland, the largest opposition party, which was previously the left-wing alliance of Labour (PvdA) and GroenLinks.

“Problems delayed”

But the VVD favoured a different package of measures designed to appeal to right-wing parties such as JA21 and the SGP, who wanted to see tax cuts instead.

The parties also had different visions of how to reform the “box 3” income tax module, which covers assets and savings, with the VVD arguing for a more generous deal for investors.

The VVD justice minister, David van Weel, said “nobody is proud of this process, nobody is happy with it” ahead of Monday’s meeting, where the draft budget was agreed.

Pro leader Jesse Klaver said he feared that the coalition parties had “not made choices” and “the problems have been delayed” until after the budget is presented on September 15.

item.title: One dead, two police officers injured in Gelderland shooting
item.description:
One dead, two police officers injured in Gelderland shooting

September 1, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

One person has died and two police officers have been injured in a shooting in Overasselt, a village in Gelderland, in the early hours of Tuesday.

Officers were called to the Ewijkseweg road in the village and taken to hospital after being injured, police said. Their condition has not been released, and no details have been given about the person who died.

Several people have been arrested, and forensic teams are searching several locations in the village. Police have not said what led to the shooting.

A resident told regional broadcaster Omroep Gelderland they heard shots at around 4.20am and saw ambulances and a trauma helicopter arrive.

item.title: Rotterdam medical students offer cash to jump training queues
item.description:
Rotterdam medical students offer cash to jump training queues

September 1, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Medical students in Rotterdam are offering each other thousands of euros to move up the queue for the hospital training they need to qualify as doctors amid a shortage of spaces.

The bids – one as high as €2,000, according to news website NU.nl – after the lottery system for places at Erasmus MC left hundreds of students waiting months, some more than a year, to begin.

The medicine master’s is built mostly around clinical placements in hospital departments. Each department can take a limited number of trainees, so start dates are drawn by lottery, and pulling the short straw can cost the better part of a year.

This time the draw went badly for a lot of them. Of the roughly 380 students who entered, about a quarter can’t start until autumn 2027 and 35% not until 2028, NU.nl reported, citing an email sent to students.

Richer students paying ahead
Students have bought and sold Rotterdam start dates before. Medisch Contact, a medical journal, documented the trade in 2020, when the medical faculty’s student council warned it let wealthier students buy their way ahead.

Erasmus MC told NU.nl it did not want money deciding who trains first, and said it would look at tightening the rules on swaps. It called the shortage of places temporary: extra students are graduating amid a switch to a new curriculum.

Students who wait longest can sometimes claim compensation from a university fund that covers study delays outside their control. The Netherlands is already facing a shortage of doctors, particularly neurologists.

item.title: Former CDA leader Elco Brinkman dies aged 78
item.description:
Former CDA leader Elco Brinkman dies aged 78

August 31, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Elco Brinkman, the Christian Democrat minister and party leader whose 1994 election defeat pushed the CDA into opposition for the first time in decades, has died aged 78. He died on Monday in Leiden after a short illness, his family said.

Brinkman became minister of welfare, health and culture in 1982, aged 34, serving seven years under Ruud Lubbers.

As minister he coined the phrase “caring society”, arguing that people had grown too dependent on the welfare state. He pushed through cuts to welfare and the arts and steered a new media law that opened the Netherlands to commercial television.

He took over as CDA leader in parliament in 1989 and was earmarked as Lubbers’s successor, but his 1994 campaign collapsed after Lubbers publicly withdrew his backing. The CDA fell from 54 seats to 34, and Brinkman left national politics in 1995.

He later chaired the construction federation Bouwend Nederland and returned as the CDA’s senate leader from 2011 to 2019.

item.title: From Sting to the beach: 12 great things to do in September
item.description:
From Sting to the beach: 12 great things to do in September

August 31, 2026 Hanneke Sanou

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The heat has receded and autumn is almost upon us. Hanneke Sanou has a round up of ideas to keep you busy in September.

Go once more unto the beach
Scheveningen is saying goodbye to a torrid summer with Live on the Beach. Whether sodden sand or glorious sunshine, the line-up will cheer up fans of Guus Meeuwis, Suzan and Freek, Acda en De Munnik, among many others. There are four live events on four consecutive days. September 3-6. Website

Get the picture
The Fotomuseum Den Haag is mounting a retrospective of 300 photographs by Eva Besnyö (1910-2003) from its own extensive collection. It follows Besnyö’s career, from Budapest to Berlin and Amsterdam, where she arrived in 1931 and where she became part of the New Photography movement which favoured dynamism and immediacy in photography.

Besnyö, who was Jewish, had to go into hiding during the war years and was active in resistance work. Her social commitment never flagged; in the 1970s she documented the Dutch feminist movement Dolle Mina. Eva Besnyö – The Liberated Camera is on from September 5. Website

Connect the dots
The Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam presents a retrospective of the work of Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama, who, it emerged last week, died on August 14 aged 97. Kusama turned her hand to everything during her long career, from painting and sculpture to performances, fashion, and literature. The show includes a new version of one of her installations executed in a characteristic black and yellow pattern, so tactile and organic, to wander round in.  From September 11. Website

Drop by the Voorlinden birthday party
The Voorlinden Museum in Wassenaar is celebrating its 10th anniversary with an exhibition which combines the museum’s favourites with equally well-loved work pilfered from other collections.

The impressive line-up of Celebrating the Icons of Art includes artists Francis Bacon, Louise Bourgeois, Alexander Calder, Nick Cave, Félix González-Torres, Damien Hirst, David Hockney, Martha Jungwirth, Mike Kelley, Yayoi Kusama, Fernand Léger, Roy Lichtenstein, Henri Matisse, Annette Messager, Joan Miró, Claude Monet, Bruce Nauman, Louise Nevelson, Lygia Pape, Gerhard Richter and Bridget Riley. From September 12. Website

Catch a monument
It’s visit-a-listed-building day, or Open Monumentendag, on September 12 and 13, when the public are invited to take a peek at special buildings, some of which are off-limits for the rest of the year.

This year’s theme is Resilient heritage in turbulent times, which puts the focus on threats such as climate change and the more pedestrian, but no less urgent, lack of finances and volunteers. Some 6,000 buildings are opening their doors, including some weird and wonderful ones like riding schools and the smallest house in Groningen. September 12 and 13. Website

Play the game
How has video game technology evolved over the years, and do video games turn people into isolated weirdos, creative problem solvers, or both? Those are the questions Game On, at the NEMO Science Museum in Amsterdam is trying to answer. For those who cannot be without their consoles, Super Nintendo, Atari 2600 and PlayStation 5 are on standby. Until October 26. Website

Get a load of Van Gogh(s)
Van Gogh lovers should head for the Kröller-Müller museum in Otterlo which has dusted off all 88 of its Van Goghs and put them all together in an exhibition for the first time in over 40 years. Built around faith, hope and charity, extolled in a sermon before he switched from preacher to painter as a profession, Van Gogh – All Our Paintings seeks to discover these virtues in the artist’s work. From September 15. Website

Don’t touch the art at Sonsbeek
“I don’t need a garden, I’m sharing a park” is the title of this year’s edition of the open-air art event in Arnhem’s Park Sonsbeek. The event features site-specific art, performances, film, and workshops by Dutch and international artists, including British-Ghanaian artist Larry Achiampong, whose work, wrapped in a pan-African flag, was recently vandalised. The torn flag will remain part of the work. Until October 11. Website

Climb the stairway to heaven
Soaring temperatures in June prevented Willem-Alexander from attempting the inaugural climb but now the spruced-up Kijk uit Attention, by Krijn Giezen (1939-2011), is open to the public once more. The attraction in the sculpture park of the Kröller-Müller museum consists of a path leading to stairs going up 87 metres, affording a view of the national Veluwe park. Website

Don’t miss
You still have a chance to catch the Rijksmuseum’s in-depth look at Dutch photographer Ed van der Elsken. The museum turned his private archive upside down in search of his methods and motivation, resulting in nine rooms covering 40 years of work, including the iconic Woman on a bike sticking out her tongue, which graces the Rijksmuseum, much to the surprise of the subject. Ed van der Elsken Up Close is on until September 13. Website

The run of Sting’s musical The Last Ship, fronted by the man himself, has been extended at Carré theatre in Amsterdam. Best be quick if you want to make it on board. Until September 13. Website

There is still time to catch the impressive but strangely titled exhibition Gerard van Honthorst – Different to Rembrandt at the Centraal Museum in Utrecht. Some 60 paintings and 30 drawings show the 17th-century master for who he was. Until September 13. Website

item.title: Beyond profit: Why Dutch firms want impact-driven leaders
item.description:
Partner content

Beyond profit: Why Dutch firms want impact-driven leaders

August 31, 2026

The Netherlands is fast becoming a testing ground for business that treats social and environmental impact as a measure of success. Its universities are adapting too: Nyenrode Business University runs an English-language Impact MBA, taught in Amsterdam and Breukelen, that builds sustainability into leadership training rather than setting it apart as a separate subject.

On April 8, 2026, the Netherlands’ National Coordinator for Sustainable Development Goals, Anna Pot, was handed a copy of the recently hashed out Impact Agenda 2030 at the Social Enterprise Government Congress in Nijmegen.

Described by the collaborative coalition of social entrepreneurs, foundations, municipal leaders, knowledge institutions and civil society initiatives that participated in its making as a “national framework for a future-proof and resilient economy”, the Impact Agenda aims to move the Dutch economy towards a system that has social and environmental metrics embedded in its core – not merely as an afterthought after profits are tallied.

“Impact is not a niche, it is a necessity,” is the message the Dutch Impact Ecosystem says it’s sending to national leaders. “And it has real economic value – for impact-driven organisations and traditional businesses alike.”

The agenda – which focusses on such themes as impact governance, procurement and finance, social and digital innovation and education and is in line with the European Commission’s Social Economy Action Plan – is just the latest national accomplishment that cements the Netherlands’ standing as a world leader in the move to sustainability and societal impact in its business sectors.

A recent report looking at how firms balance profit with impact found that of the 77 large companies the private-public consortium surveyed doing business in the Netherlands, the majority believe the initial regulatory hassles of the EU’s CSRD [Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive] are overshadowed by its long-term benefits, all while helping their businesses.

The report found that “Dutch companies are leading the way in integrating impact governance into their strategies.”

Learning laboratory

The country’s strong collaborations between businesses, government and knowledge institutions create an environment of innovation and entrepreneurship that has led professionals worldwide to increasingly choose the Netherlands to learn how businesses can create both commercial success and positive societal change.

In the Netherlands’ dynamic Dutch business ecosystem, leaders have the opportunity to put theory into practice.

New leaders

Driven by European sustainability regulations, evolving investor expectations, rapid technological developments such as AI and growing stakeholder expectations, companies today are looking for leaders who can navigate complexity rather than optimize a single bottom line.

And the country’s universities and knowledge institutions are keeping pace. Nyenrode Business University, with locations in Amsterdam and Breukelen, offers an English-language MBA program focused on creating the future leaders of this brave new business world.

Its Impact MBA was designed as a response to changing employer needs rather than as a traditional MBA program. Instead of teaching sustainability as a standalone subject, the curriculum integrates leadership, digital transformation and sustainability throughout the learning experience.

“Sustainability transitions involve long-term developments with significant short-term implications for organizations,” says Prof. Dr. Nicolas Chevrollier, Professor of Sustainability Transitions and designer of the Impact MBA. “This requires new competences, new collaborations and sometimes entirely new business models.”

Chevrollier emphasises that organizations cannot solve today’s challenges independently. Businesses increasingly operate within ecosystems involving governments, knowledge institutions, investors and civil society, meaning effective leadership depends on building partnerships rather than optimising organisations in isolation. 

“Many organisations suffer from tunnel vision,” he says. “To truly innovate, leaders need to broaden their perspective.”

The Impact MBA gives tomorrow’s leaders a chance to do just that: innovation and a systems-thinking approach are embedded in its curriculum, creating business trailblazers who can balance financial and societal objectives while thinking across entire systems instead of just individual organizations.

Are you looking to develop the new capabilities needed for the profound transformations taking place in today’s business world? Then check out Nyenrode ‘s Impact MBA, available both part-time and full-time, or join one of their on-campus and online events to discover more.

item.title: Large explosion at restaurant in Utrecht
item.description:
Large explosion at restaurant in Utrecht

August 31, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A major explosion occurred early Monday morning at a barbecue restaurant in Utrecht, according to local broadcaster RTV Utrecht.

The blast went off at 1am at the Topkapi restaurant, shattering windows and destroying the front of the building.

No one was injured but nearby residents were evacuated as a precaution.

The restaurant was the target of another bombing in 2023. A 19-year-old from Utrecht was later convicted of the crime. According to the court, he had attempted to extort money from the restaurant’s owner.

The police would not comment on a motivation and are investigating.

item.title: Coalition budget talks still deadlocked with hours to go
item.description:
Coalition budget talks still deadlocked with hours to go

August 31, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Plans to cut more than €6 billion from social security and to change the way savings and investments are taxed are in the balance, as the three coalition parties struggle to agree next year’s budget among themselves with only hours to go before it is due for review.

D66, the VVD and the CDA negotiated through the whole of Sunday and into the early hours of Monday without reaching a deal, and are still talking on Monday afternoon. The meeting at which the full cabinet has to sign off the budget, first scheduled for 11am, has been put back twice and is now set for 6pm.

Until last week, the main question was whether the minority coalition could win enough opposition votes to pass the budget. Prime minister Rob Jetten ended those talks on Friday, saying the plans would go to parliament without a majority.

That has left the coalition parties to settle the budget between themselves, and they remain divided. Jetten acknowledged on Friday that the three parties still disagree fundamentally on some key points.

What they are arguing over
Broadcaster NOS reported that two issues are holding up a deal: the box 3 tax and the planned social security cuts.

Box 3 is the tax on income from savings and investments, which the government has been trying to reform for years. The coalition’s spending plans also include cutting more than €6 billion from social security – the benefits paid to people who are unemployed, older or too ill to work.

The largest opposition party, the left-wing PRO, has made scrapping that cut a condition of its support and wants wealthy households taxed more instead. Led by Jesse Klaver, PRO already won a concession from the government this year, when it dropped a plan to raise the retirement age more quickly.

D66 and the CDA want to avoid tilting the budget too far to the right, so as to keep PRO within reach. The VVD is wary of concessions to the left that could sour its relations with the far-right JA21 and the orthodox Protestant SGP.

The coalition could pass the budget through the lower house with JA21 and SGP support, but that combination would leave it well short in the senate, where PRO’s backing offers the more realistic route to a majority.

The draft is due at the Council of State, which reviews the plans before they are presented on Prinsjesdag on September 15.

item.title: The number of English-language bookstores is on the rise
item.description:
The number of English-language bookstores is on the rise

August 31, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Thanks in part to social media, the number of English-language books read in the Netherlands is increasing, and with it, the number of shops catering to those bookworms.

One in five books sold in the Netherlands is in English, according to industry monitor KVB Boekwerk. Broadcaster NOS reported that over the past four years, at least ten new English-language bookshops have opened their doors in the country, including in Tilburg, Utrecht and Amersfoort.

The increase is attributed in large part to social media, particularly the popularity of BookTok, a community of content creators making videos primarily about books.

Many bookstores now stock books popular on BookTok and have entire displays of what’s currently going viral online.

These new shops are often operated by people who came from outside of the publishing world. Daan Severijns changed course after a career in IT. He runs Books and Beans in Tilburg together with his partner Ana Maria Vallejo Perez .

“We used to philosophise about what we would like to do after retirement: run a small bookstore in a beautiful location. Then I lost my job, and the wish quickly grew into what it is today,” he told NOS.

item.title: Big cities buckling under homelessness and drugs, says Halsema
item.description:
Big cities buckling under homelessness and drugs, says Halsema

August 31, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Amsterdam mayor Femke Halsema has called on the government to take national action on rising homelessness, crack addiction and public disorder, warning that they are eroding quality of life in the country’s biggest cities and cannot be tackled by city authorities alone.

Speaking in an interview with Het Parool and on current-affairs programme Buitenhof, Halsema said the same pressures were affecting all four big cities – Amsterdam, Rotterdam, The Hague and Utrecht – and that the government was partly responsible.

“The problems in the big cities are gradually overwhelming us,” she said, calling for “major measures” from The Hague.

Amsterdam has 3,644 recorded people who cause public disorder, Halsema said, though she stressed the number of homeless people is far higher. The most recent count, in 2024, recorded more than 15,000 people in the Amsterdam region as homeless or at risk of losing their home, though the city says the true figure is higher.

“Public poverty”
The most visible problems come from a combination of homelessness and crack use, particularly in the city’s parks, which Halsema said was distressing residents and traumatising for the addicts themselves.

She said that debates in The Hague ahead of the budget focus on income and taxation, while cities are left dealing with “public poverty”: the visible result of underfunded services, the housing shortage and a strain on the mental health care system.

She wants the government to structurally improve mental health provision and overhaul rules governing foreign workers.

Foreign workers
About 1,500 of the people causing nuisance come from eastern Europe, according to Halsema, many of them foreign workers who end up losing their housing and their jobs because the two are tied together. Amsterdam organisations have previously helped hundreds return home, a significant number of them crack users.

Employers in the Netherlands are allowed to house foreign workers while deducting the cost from their wages, currently up to a quarter of the minimum wage. Former social affairs minister Mariëlle Paul ended a planned phase-out of that rule last year, a decision Halsema branded “disastrous”.

She wants the rule reversed, faster action against rogue employment agencies, and more money for shelter: of the €13 million she said was made available last year for housing foreign workers, Amsterdam received €2 million, which she said is far too little.

Sleeping outdoors
Amsterdam stopped fining people for sleeping outdoors in June last year and, like Utrecht, now wants to decriminalise it entirely. Halsema says fines only push homeless people further into debt and further from help.

Police have raised concerns about that approach. In a review by the local health service in April, officers said people were coming to Amsterdam because they were allowed to sleep outdoors there, and that police and other enforcement teams had fewer tools to steer them towards help.

With annual budget talks ongoing, Halsema said the government must act: “Enable us to make sure our city is in order and liveable.”
